section.title: The Queen of Sheba and Solomon's Death
section.sectionRationale: A foreign queen travels a great distance to test Solomon's famous wisdom with hard questions, and what she finds leaves her breathless, taking her breath away with wonder at his wisdom, wealth, and the ordered devotion of his household and his worship. The chapter then surveys Solomon's staggering wealth, his golden throne, his fleets, and his fame among all the kings of the earth, before closing simply with his death after forty years on the throne.
section.thesis: The queen of Sheba's confession that the report of Solomon's wisdom did not tell even half the truth, followed by a summary of unmatched wealth and honor, and then the plain, sobering notice of Solomon's death, together show that even the greatest of Israel's kings, blessed beyond any other, still could not escape the common end of all flesh, pointing forward to a King greater than Solomon whose reign will never end.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the queen of Sheba's visit and confession, verses 1 to 12; Solomon's wealth, throne, and fame, verses 13 to 28; and the closing summary and death of Solomon, verses 29 to 31.

units.label: The queen of Sheba's visit and confession
units.note: not half the greatness was told to me

verses.text: Now when the queen of Sheba heard about the fame of Solomon, she came to test him with difficult questions. She arrived in Jerusalem with a very large caravan, with camels bearing spices, gold in abundance, and precious stones. And she came to Solomon and spoke with him about all that was on her mind.
And Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was too difficult for him to explain.
When the queen of Sheba saw the {{chokmah|wisdom}} of Solomon, the palace he had built,

the food at his table, the seating of his servants, the service and attire of his attendants, the attire of his cupbearers, and the burnt offerings he presented at the house of the LORD, it took her breath away.
She said to the king, "The report I heard in my own country about your words and wisdom is true.
But I did not believe the reports until I came and saw with my own eyes. Indeed, not half of the greatness of your wisdom was told to me. You have far exceeded the report I heard.
How blessed are your men! How blessed are these servants of yours who stand continually before you and hear your wisdom!

Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you to set you on His throne to be king for the LORD your God. Because your God loved Israel enough to establish them forever, He has made you king over them to carry out {{mishpat|justice}} and righteousness."
Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, a great quantity of spices, and precious stones. There had never been such spices as those the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.
The servants of Hiram and of Solomon who brought gold from Ophir also brought algum wood and precious stones.

The king made the algum wood into steps for the house of the LORD and for the king's palace, and into lyres and harps for the singers. Never before had anything like them been seen in the land of Judah.
King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba all she desired, whatever she asked, far more than she had brought the king. Then she left and returned to her own country, along with her servants.
The weight of gold that came to Solomon each year was 666 talents,
not including the revenue from the merchants and traders. And all the Arabian kings and governors of the land also brought gold and silver to Solomon.
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of hammered gold; six hundred shekels of hammered gold went into each shield.
He also made three hundred small shields of hammered gold; three hundred shekels of gold went into each shield. And the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
Additionally, the king made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with pure gold.
The throne had six steps, and a footstool of gold was attached to it. There were armrests on both sides of the seat, with a lion standing beside each armrest.
Twelve lions stood on the six steps, one at either end of each step. Nothing like this had ever been made for any kingdom.
All King Solomon's drinking cups were gold, and all the utensils of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. There was no silver, because it was accounted as nothing in the days of Solomon.
For the king had the ships of Tarshish that went with Hiram's servants, and once every three years the ships of Tarshish would arrive bearing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
So King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom.
All the kings of the earth sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart.
Year after year, each visitor would bring his tribute: articles of silver and gold, clothing, weapons, spices, horses, and mules.
Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots, and 12,000 horses, which he stationed in the chariot cities and also with him in Jerusalem.
He reigned over all the kings from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines, as far as the border of Egypt.
The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as abundant as sycamore in the foothills.
Solomon's horses were imported from Egypt and from all the lands.

As for the rest of the acts of Solomon, from beginning to end, are they not written in the Records of Nathan the Prophet, in the Prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the Visions of Iddo the Seer concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat?
Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years.
And Solomon {{shakab|rested}} with his fathers and was buried in the city of his father David. And his son Rehoboam reigned in his place.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom. It is Solomon's chokmah, first requested at Gibeon in chapter 1, that draws the queen of Sheba across a great distance, and it is this same wisdom, along with the ordered devotion she observes in his household and worship, that leaves her breathless with astonishment.

mishpat.gloss: Justice, judgment, right ruling. The queen recognizes that God made Solomon king specifically to carry out mishpat and righteousness, naming the very purpose for which wisdom was granted in the first place, back in chapter 1, to govern God's people well.

shakab.gloss: To lie down, to rest. The chapter's closing note that Solomon shakab, rested, with his fathers is the common, sober biblical idiom for death, a plain reminder that even the wisest and wealthiest king Israel ever knew still lay down at last among mortal men.

basic.context: The queen of Sheba, hearing of Solomon's fame, travels a great distance with a vast caravan of spices, gold, and precious stones to test him with hard questions. What she sees, his wisdom, his palace, his ordered household, and his worship at the temple, leaves her breathless, and she confesses that the reports she had heard did not even tell half the truth. The chapter then catalogs Solomon's staggering wealth, his golden throne with its twelve lions, his fleets bringing exotic treasures every three years, and his fame among all the kings of the earth, before closing simply and soberly: after forty years, Solomon rested with his fathers and died.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative recording a specific royal visit and a summary of Solomon's reign; it is not a promise that wisdom automatically produces limitless wealth for every believer today. What is theologically significant is the juxtaposition the chapter creates: unmatched wisdom and wealth, praised even by a foreign queen who recognizes God's hand in it, followed immediately by the plain fact of death, showing that no earthly splendor, however God given, escapes mortality.
basic.originalLanguages: It is Solomon's chokmah, wisdom, that draws the queen across such a distance, and she recognizes that God gave it to him precisely so he could carry out mishpat, justice, and righteousness for his people. The chapter's final word on Solomon is that he shakab, rested, with his fathers, the Bible's common, unadorned way of naming death, even for the greatest of kings.
basic.typology: Jesus Himself points to this chapter, declaring that something greater than Solomon is here, Matthew 12:42, since the queen of Sheba traveled far to hear wisdom that would one day pale before the wisdom and person of Christ, freely available to all who seek Him. Solomon's wealth, wisdom, and fame among all the kings of the earth anticipate the greater King before whom every nation will one day bow, and whose reign, unlike Solomon's forty years, will never end.
basic.christ: Jesus explicitly invokes this queen, saying the Queen of the South will rise up in judgment and condemn this generation, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom, and now something greater than Solomon is here, Matthew 12:42. Solomon's wealth and honor, unmatched among earthly kings, are a shadow of the greater glory and kingdom that belong to Christ, the true Son of David whose throne, unlike Solomon's ivory and gold one, will be established forever, Luke 1:32-33.
basic.god: God delights to bless obedient wisdom generously, so much that even foreign rulers recognize His hand and bless Him for it. Yet God's Word does not shy away from recording, with plain honesty, that even Solomon, the most blessed king Israel ever had, still died like every other man, a sober reminder that all human glory is temporary, and lasting hope must rest in the God who reigns beyond any single king's lifetime.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Kings 10 gives the parallel account of the queen of Sheba's visit and Solomon's wealth. Matthew 12:42 records Jesus declaring that something, and someone, greater than Solomon is here. Luke 1:32-33 promises that Christ's throne and kingdom will have no end, unlike Solomon's forty year reign. And Ecclesiastes, traditionally linked to Solomon's own reflection late in life, wrestles honestly with the fleeting nature of even the greatest earthly achievement.
basic.oneStory: The queen of Sheba's astonished confession and the catalog of Solomon's unmatched wealth mark the high point of Israel's earthly kingdom, yet the chapter's final, understated sentence, Solomon rested with his fathers and died, quietly insists that no earthly splendor lasts forever. The whole scene points forward to Christ, the true and greater Son of David, before whom every nation will one day marvel, and whose throne, unlike any human king's, will never come to an end.

context.literary:
The chapter's three movements grow shorter and colder as they proceed. The queen's visit occupies twelve verses of direct speech and personal encounter, verses 1 to 12; the survey of wealth and fame occupies sixteen verses of impersonal cataloguing, gold totals, shield counts, horse numbers, verses 13 to 28, with no named individual after the queen departs; and the reign's end occupies three verses of bare notice, a source citation, a regnal total, and a burial formula, verses 29 to 31. The effect is almost cinematic, a scene pulling back from intimate conversation to aerial inventory to a closing title card, each stage further from the human warmth of the opening encounter.

The middle section itself is built from lists rather than narrative, gold by the talent, shields by the shekel, lions by the pair, horses by the thousand, a style closer to a royal archive's ledger than to storytelling. That flatness is deliberate. A reader who has just heard the queen's breathless confession, not half the greatness of your wisdom was told to me, verse 6, is handed page after page of proof, numbers piled on numbers, as if the text itself wants to overwhelm the reader the way Solomon overwhelmed his visitor.

Then, without warning or transition, all of it stops. Verse 29 turns immediately to source citations, the kind of formula Chronicles uses to close nearly every royal reign, and verse 31 states the end as plainly as it states anything else in the chapter, Solomon rested with his fathers and died. No lament, no eulogy, no reflection interrupts the record's own momentum; the same flat, cataloguing voice that listed shields and horses now lists a death, refusing the reader any more ceremony for the ending than it gave to the throne's twelve lions.
context.historical:
Sheba is best identified with the south Arabian kingdom of Saba, centered in what is now Yemen, a major hub controlling the overland incense and spice trade that carried frankincense and myrrh north toward the Mediterranean. A camel caravan bearing spices, gold, and precious stones, verse 1, matches what is known of Sabaean commercial expeditions, and a state built on that trade had every reason to investigate, and perhaps negotiate access through, the kingdom now controlling the northern end of its trade routes under Solomon.

The scale of the numbers in this chapter, 666 talents of gold yearly, verse 13, twelve thousand horses, verse 25, silver as common as stones, verse 27, would represent an extraordinary concentration of wealth by the standard of any ancient Near Eastern kingdom, comparable to or exceeding what is known of contemporary Egyptian or Mesopotamian royal treasuries at their height. Whether or not every figure is meant with modern statistical precision, the numbers function rhetorically as much as historically, communicating an order of wealth so far beyond ordinary royal means that no reader in the ancient world could mistake the claim being made about Solomon's unmatched standing among the kings of the earth, verse 22.

The horses imported from Egypt, verse 28, moved through an established trade corridor; horse and chariot exports northward into the Levant are a known commercial pattern of the age, so this detail reflects an ordinary feature of ancient trade rather than an isolated claim unique to Solomon's court.
context.canonical:
This chapter reads as the fulfillment of a trajectory that began quietly in the previous chapter. Deuteronomy's law for Israel's king had specifically warned against a king who multiplies horses for himself, especially by trade with Egypt, and one who accumulates for himself great quantities of silver and gold, Deuteronomy 17:16-17. Chapter 8 recorded the first steps in that direction almost in passing; this chapter supplies the completed numbers, twelve thousand horses partly imported from Egypt, verse 28, and 666 talents of gold arriving every single year, verse 13, without the surrounding narrative ever pausing to measure the total against the law that had warned against exactly this outcome.

The chapter also sits in careful relationship to 1 Kings, which records the same visit and the same wealth in chapter 10 before moving directly into Solomon's foreign wives and apostasy in chapter 11. Chronicles reproduces almost everything from 1 Kings 10 but stops precisely where Kings turns dark, omitting 1 Kings 11 entirely and moving straight from wealth and fame to the bare fact of death. The effect is to let Solomon's story end, in Chronicles' own telling, on its highest note rather than its lowest, even though any reader who also knew Kings, as the Chronicler's first audience certainly did, would hear the silence about Solomon's later years as its own kind of commentary.

Centuries later this chapter becomes the direct background for one of Jesus' own arguments. When He tells His hearers that the Queen of the South will rise up in judgment against them, Matthew 12:42 and Luke 11:31, He is not introducing a new figure but assuming His audience already knows this very story well enough to feel the force of the comparison immediately.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Chronicler wanted his readers, themselves living without a king and without anything resembling Solomon's wealth, to see in this chapter the outer limit of what faithful wisdom, generously blessed by God, could produce in a human kingdom, an outsider's own astonished testimony serving as confirmation that Israel's God, and the king He had raised up, exceeded anything the watching nations had imagined. At the same time, by ending the chapter, and with it his entire account of Solomon, on the bare notice of death rather than any celebration of legacy, the Chronicler quietly reminds the same readers that no accumulation of wealth, wisdom, or fame secures a future beyond a single human lifetime.

The two purposes work together rather than against each other: Solomon's glory really was extraordinary and really did testify to God's blessing, and that same glory still ended exactly where every other king's glory ends, so that hope for something beyond a forty year reign could not, even at its most spectacular, be placed in Solomon himself.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what happened during a specific reign; it does not promise that wisdom will always produce this scale of wealth, nor does it instruct kings, or anyone else, to pursue horses, gold, and foreign trade as evidence of God's favor. Read alongside Deuteronomy 17:16-17, several of the very details this chapter reports with evident pride, the horse count, the gold total, read less like commendation and more like documentation of a king outgrowing the limits his own law had set for him, without the text stopping to say so directly.

Discernment is required to separate the chapter's plain historical claims, a queen visited, gifts were exchanged, wealth accumulated, from its implied evaluation, which is not uniformly positive once the numbers are set beside Israel's own covenant standards for kingship, a tension the chapter leaves for attentive readers to notice rather than resolving for them outright.

debates.question: Why does the Chronicler omit Solomon's later apostasy, recorded in 1 Kings 11, from his account?

views.label: A deliberate idealized portrait for a struggling community
views.case: Writing for exiles without a king or a full temple, the Chronicler consistently emphasizes positive models of faithfulness; omitting Solomon's decline lets his account of Solomon's reign stand as an encouraging pattern of wisdom and temple centered worship rather than a cautionary tale, which the Chronicler reserves for other kings.

views.label: A theological rather than a comprehensive historical purpose
views.case: The Chronicler's stated sources, verse 29, indicate a fuller record existed elsewhere; his own selection is deliberately theological, tracing the temple and covenant themes rather than attempting an exhaustive biography, so the omission reflects purpose rather than ignorance or concealment.

debates.bearing: Both views agree the omission is intentional and consistent with the Chronicler's larger purpose, using Solomon's reign to model wisdom, worship, and the blessings that flow from seeking God, while the plain fact of Solomon's death still closes the account with appropriate sobriety.

debates.question: Does this chapter present Solomon's horses, gold, and silver as unqualified blessing, or as a quiet warning once measured against Deuteronomy 17:16-17?

views.label: Straightforward commendation of God's blessing
views.case: The chapter's own vocabulary is uniformly positive, surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom, verse 22, with no hint of criticism attached to any figure; the Chronicler consistently presents material blessing as the natural fruit of covenant faithfulness, and nothing in the immediate context signals that this case should be read differently.

views.label: A quiet echo of the king's forbidden excess
views.case: The specific categories named, horses multiplied and partly sourced from Egypt, verse 28, and silver and gold accumulated on a scale the text itself calls unprecedented, verses 20 and 27, match Deuteronomy 17:16-17's prohibitions closely enough that a reader familiar with the Torah would likely notice the resemblance, especially once 1 Kings 11, whether or not Chronicles repeats it, is known to follow immediately after.

debates.bearing: The chapter does not resolve the tension itself, and readers need not choose only one option; Solomon's wealth can be genuinely a sign of God's blessing on wisdom rightly sought, 1 Kings 3:11-13, and still, in its eventual excess, a warning of how easily blessing given can become an appetite pursued for its own sake.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the three words already named, several other details in the Hebrew repay attention. Verse 4 says the sight of Solomon's court took her breath away, an English rendering of an idiom whose underlying sense is closer to there was no more ruach left in her, ruach being the same word Hebrew uses for breath, wind, and spirit depending on context. The queen is not merely impressed; the text pictures her as emptied of the very breath, ruach, that had carried her all the way from Sheba, an image of being overwhelmed so completely that the word for ordinary respiration and the word for spiritual vitality briefly coincide.

Verse 8 praises God for setting Solomon on the throne to carry out mishpat and tsedaqah, justice and righteousness, a fixed word pair rather than two loosely associated virtues. The same paired formula describes the ideal of David's own reign, 2 Samuel 8:15, and becomes the defining hope of the coming messianic king in Isaiah, who will reign on David's throne, upholding it with justice and righteousness from that time on and forevermore, Isaiah 9:7. The queen's compliment is not generic royal flattery; she names, in the exact stock language of Israel's own royal ideal, the two qualities every future king of David's line would be measured against.

The gold this chapter measures obsessively is counted in kikkar, talents, a unit whose name literally means a circle or round object, describing the shape of the cast ingot rather than an abstract measure of weight. Six hundred and sixty six kikkar of gold arriving in a single year, verse 13, or 450 kikkar carried home by Hiram's fleet in the previous chapter, are pictured, quite concretely in the word itself, as stacks of round metal disks rather than a figure on a ledger, a detail that may explain why the text can say silver was accounted as nothing, verse 20, once gold had become common enough to count only in circles of this size.

Finally, the chapter's closing formula, Solomon shakab, rested, with his fathers, verse 31, is the standard succession language Kings and Chronicles use for nearly every king who dies a natural death, not a phrase reserved for Solomon's dignity alone. Its very ordinariness is part of its force. Scripture reserves different language entirely for the rare figures it wants to mark as exceptions to death's usual pattern, God took Enoch, so that he was not found, Genesis 5:24, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven, 2 Kings 2:11. Solomon receives no such exception. The same formula that will close the reign of nearly every king after him closes his as well, wisdom, wealth, and fame notwithstanding.

typology.type: The queen traveling from the ends of the earth to test Solomon's wisdom
typology.fulfillment: The queen came from the ends of the earth, on her own initiative, at great cost and personal risk, simply to test whether the reports about Solomon's wisdom could possibly be true. Jesus turns this history into an indictment: she will rise at the judgment and condemn the very generation privileged to hear One greater than Solomon without having to travel anywhere at all, Matthew 12:42. The type escalates by inversion. Where the queen crossed a continent to reach wisdom, wisdom itself, in Christ, now stands in front of people who need only listen, making their indifference far less excusable than her costly pilgrimage.

typology.type: Solomon's unmatched wealth, throne, and fame among the kings of the earth
typology.fulfillment: Solomon's fame drew every king of the earth to seek an audience with him, verse 23, yet that same fame could not outlast a single human lifetime, closing three verses later with his death. Philippians pictures a throne whose fame will produce a far more complete response than mere royal visits, every knee bowing and every tongue confessing Jesus Christ is Lord, Philippians 2:10-11, not because visitors happened to hear a favorable report but because the whole created order will finally recognize what it owes its true King. Unlike Solomon's forty years, that recognition never has to end in a closing verse.

typology.type: The queen's confession, not half the greatness of your wisdom was told to me
typology.fulfillment: Solomon's reputation reached Sheba only in partial report, and even firsthand experience exceeded what rumor had prepared her to expect. Paul describes Christ as the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, Colossians 2:3, and calls the riches found in Him unsearchable, unable to be fully traced out or exhausted, Ephesians 3:8. John goes further still, admitting that even a complete written record of everything Jesus did could not be contained in the world's own libraries, John 21:25. What was true in degree of Solomon, that no report does justice to the reality, is true without limit of Christ.

study.christ:
Solomon did not possess wisdom as his own natural attribute; he asked God for it and received it as a gift beyond what he requested, riches and honor besides, 1 Kings 3:11-13. Christ is presented in the New Testament not as one who received wisdom from another but as wisdom itself, the power of God and the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24, in whom, Paul says, are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Colossians 2:3. The difference in category matters. The queen tested Solomon's wisdom with hard questions and found it sufficient; no one tests Christ's wisdom and finds Him merely sufficient, because He does not hold wisdom, He is the wisdom every other wise word in Scripture ultimately serves.

The gifts the queen brought, gold, spices, and precious stones, verse 9, anticipate a scene centuries later when magi from a similarly distant eastern region arrive with gold, frankincense, and myrrh for a different king, Matthew 2:11, though this time the king they honor is an infant with no fortified cities, no fleet, and no throne of ivory to His name. The pattern of distant seekers bringing costly gifts because of a king's reported greatness repeats, but the king they find in Bethlehem possesses nothing of Solomon's visible splendor, His greatness hidden rather than displayed, recognized by faith rather than confirmed by an inspection tour of palaces and stables.

The chapter's ending is where the contrast becomes sharpest. Solomon's forty year reign closes with the plainest possible sentence, he rested with his fathers and died, verse 31, and a son takes his place because that is what death always requires. Hebrews explains that there have been many other priests, since death prevented them from continuing in office, but because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood, Hebrews 7:23-24. Solomon needed a Rehoboam to succeed him. Christ needs no successor, because the death that ended Solomon's reign could not hold Him, and the throne Gabriel promises Mary's son, unlike the ivory one with its twelve lions, will never pass to anyone else, Luke 1:32-33.

Even Solomon's fame among all the kings of the earth, verse 23, drawing visitors who came merely to hear him, anticipates but falls short of what Scripture promises Christ will receive without any visitor needing to travel first: every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, Philippians 2:10-11, a homage owed not to reported wisdom but to the risen and exalted Son Himself.
study.god:
This chapter records one of the earliest scenes in Scripture where a Gentile ruler, unprompted by any Israelite missionary effort, travels a great distance and ends up blessing Israel's God in her own words, blessed be the LORD your God, verse 8. She is not the first foreigner to do this, Rahab confesses that the LORD is God in heaven above and on earth below, Joshua 2:11, and Naaman later declares that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel, 2 Kings 5:15, but the queen's confession is unusually reasoned rather than merely reactive to a miracle; she examines the evidence herself, tests it with hard questions, and concludes that Israel's God, not merely Israel's king, deserves credit for what she has seen. Long before the prophets make the ingathering of the nations an explicit promise, this chapter shows God already at work drawing a foreign ruler to recognize Him through nothing more dramatic than observed wisdom and order.

The chapter is also careful, in verse 23, to say the wisdom that draws every king of the earth is wisdom that God had put in his heart, keeping the source of Solomon's achievement in view even at the height of the impersonal wealth catalog that follows. Solomon accumulates gold, horses, and shields by the hundreds, but the text never once credits Solomon's own genius as the ultimate explanation; even the numbers that follow rest on a gift already given rather than a talent Solomon generated for himself.

Yet the God of this chapter also lets the plain fact of death stand at the end of all that wealth without editorial comment, a silence that is itself theological. Paul later instructs those who are rich not to be conceited or to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth but in God, who richly provides all things to enjoy, 1 Timothy 6:17, precisely the lesson this chapter teaches by its structure rather than by direct statement. The narrative does not need to moralize explicitly about the dangers of wealth when it can simply let sixteen verses of golden shields and ivory thrones collapse, without transition, into three verses ending in a grave.

God, in other words, is shown here to be generous without being sentimental about what that generosity produces. He gives wisdom and wealth beyond any king's asking, exactly as He promised at Gibeon, 1 Kings 3:11-13, and He also lets that same wealth expire on schedule with its recipient, refusing to let even Solomon's story suggest that abundance, however genuinely given by God, ever becomes a substitute for the God who gave it.

crossReferences.note: Kings tells the same story of the queen's visit and Solomon's wealth in almost identical detail, though it immediately follows this account with Solomon's foreign wives and eventual idolatry in chapter 11, material Chronicles chooses not to repeat in its own version of these same events.

At Gibeon Solomon asked only for wisdom to govern well, and God granted that request while adding riches and honor he had not requested, the origin of the very wealth this chapter spends sixteen verses cataloguing in exhaustive, almost breathless detail.

The king's law forbade multiplying horses, especially through Egypt, and accumulating silver and gold; this chapter's twelve thousand horses partly imported from Egypt and its yearly gold income of 666 talents describe, without comment, a king who has now done precisely what that law once warned against.

The chapter Chronicles never reaches records that Solomon's heart was eventually turned after other gods by the very wives and alliances his wealth and fame had made possible, showing where the trajectory this chapter celebrates was already quietly heading even as the queen offered her praise.

Traditionally read as Solomon's own late reflection on his life, this passage catalogs building projects, silver, gold, and pleasures on a scale matching this chapter's own inventory, only to conclude that all of it was futile, a pursuit of the wind, a verdict the king who built it all reaches about himself.

Luke records the same saying about the Queen of the South rising in judgment that Matthew records, confirming that Jesus returned to this very episode more than once as a settled example of a diligent seeker whose journey exposes the indifference of those who will not travel even the shortest distance toward greater wisdom.

Paul's instruction to the rich, not to be conceited or to hope in the uncertainty of wealth but in God who provides it, reads like a commentary written in advance on a chapter that lets Solomon's staggering fortune end, three verses later, in an ordinary grave.

Paul says all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ, language that echoes, and quietly surpasses, a chapter built entirely around a queen's search for treasures of wisdom she had to travel to Jerusalem, and still could not fully access.

Solomon's forty year reign required a successor because death ended it on schedule, exactly the pattern Hebrews contrasts with Christ, who holds His priesthood permanently for the simple reason that, unlike every king this chapter or any other Israelite chronicle records, He continues forever.

study.oneStory:
Long before this chapter, God had promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, and the prophets will later picture that promise fulfilled as a flood of nations streaming toward Zion, bringing their wealth with them, kings coming to the brightness of its dawn, camels of Midian and Ephah covering the land, and all from Sheba bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praises of the LORD, Isaiah 60:3-6. The queen of Sheba's caravan of spices, gold, and precious stones, arriving decades or centuries before Isaiah ever wrote those words, reads like a small, real, historical down payment on a promise not yet spoken, one nation's wealth flowing toward Jerusalem long before the prophets describe it as the pattern for every nation.

But this chapter also marks a hinge in the opposite direction. Everything before it in Solomon's story moves toward completion, the temple built, the glory descended, the kingdom secured, the nations impressed. Everything after it, beginning in the next chapter with Rehoboam's folly, moves toward division, decline, and eventually exile, the very fate this book's own audience had already lived through by the time they read it. Solomon's death, reported here in the plainest possible terms, is the pivot on which that whole downward arc turns, so that the chapter functions as both a summit and the first step down from it in the very same three verses.

The rest of the Bible keeps holding these two threads together, the promise that the nations will one day come, and the sober fact that no human king can hold a kingdom together across generations by wisdom or wealth alone. Both threads resolve in Christ. He is the true and final King to whom the nations stream, not because they hear a report of His wisdom secondhand but because He has been raised and exalted, and He is also the King whose reign genuinely will not end in a closing verse about death, since death itself could not hold Him, and His throne, unlike Solomon's, requires no chapter thirty to begin its decline.

quiz.q: Why did the queen of Sheba travel to Jerusalem?

options.text: To test Solomon with hard questions after hearing of his fame and wisdom.
options.note: Verse 1 states this explicitly as the purpose of her journey.

options.text: To form a military alliance against a common enemy.
options.note: The text presents her visit as a quest to test Solomon's wisdom, not a military alliance.

options.text: To demand tribute from Solomon.
options.note: She brought lavish gifts to Solomon rather than demanding tribute from him, verse 9.

options.text: The chapter gives no reason for her visit.
options.note: Verse 1 explicitly states her reason for coming.

quiz.q: What was the queen of Sheba's response after seeing Solomon's wisdom and household firsthand?

options.text: She confessed that not even half the greatness of his wisdom had been told to her, and she blessed the LORD for setting Solomon on the throne to carry out justice and righteousness.
options.note: Verses 6-8 record this full confession.

options.text: She dismissed the reports as exaggerated and unimpressive.
options.note: The opposite occurred; she found the reality exceeded the reports, not fell short of them.

options.text: She demanded that Solomon abandon the worship of the LORD.
options.note: She instead blessed the LORD, Solomon's God, verse 8.

options.text: The chapter records no reaction from her at all.
options.note: Verses 5-8 record an extensive, detailed reaction and confession.

quiz.q: What details describe the scale of Solomon's wealth in this chapter?

options.text: 666 talents of gold arrived each year, silver was as common as stones, and his throne of ivory and gold was unmatched by any kingdom.
options.note: Verses 13, 15-20, and 27 all describe this staggering wealth in detail.

options.text: Solomon lived modestly, avoiding excessive wealth or display.
options.note: The chapter describes the opposite, an unprecedented scale of wealth and display.

options.text: Solomon's wealth came entirely from military conquest.
options.note: The wealth described comes from trade, tribute, and gifts, not conquest, as detailed in verses 9, 14, and 21-24.

options.text: The chapter contains no description of Solomon's wealth.
options.note: Verses 13-28 are an extended catalog of Solomon's wealth.

options.text: With the simple, sober notice that after forty years reigning in Jerusalem, Solomon rested with his fathers and died, and his son Rehoboam succeeded him.
options.note: Verses 29-31 record this plain closing statement.

options.text: With a lengthy account of a national celebration honoring Solomon's achievements.
options.note: The chapter's ending is notably brief and sober, not an extended celebration.

options.text: With a description of Solomon's temple being destroyed.
options.note: The temple's destruction comes centuries later, in 2 Chronicles 36, not at the end of this chapter.

options.text: The chapter never mentions Solomon's death.
options.note: Verse 31 explicitly records Solomon's death and burial.

quiz.q: How does Jesus later refer to this chapter's account of the queen of Sheba?

options.text: He says the Queen of the South will rise up in judgment against an unbelieving generation, since she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom, and something greater than Solomon is here.
options.note: Matthew 12:42 records Jesus making this exact connection.

options.text: Jesus never references the queen of Sheba or Solomon's wisdom anywhere in the Gospels.
options.note: Matthew 12:42 explicitly references her, directly connecting this chapter to Jesus' own teaching.

options.text: Jesus criticizes the queen of Sheba for her lack of faith.
options.note: Jesus commends her diligence in seeking wisdom, using her as a positive example against an unbelieving generation, not as a criticism of her.

options.text: Jesus claims Solomon's wisdom was never real.
options.note: Jesus affirms Solomon's wisdom while declaring that something even greater than it is now present in Himself.

questions: The queen of Sheba traveled a great distance to seek wisdom firsthand rather than relying only on reports. What truth about God have you only heard secondhand that you need to seek and test for yourself?
She confessed that the reality exceeded everything she had been told. When has your own experience of God's goodness exceeded what you expected or had been told?
Solomon's wealth was staggering, yet the chapter ends simply with his death. What does this teach you about where to place your ultimate hope, wealth and achievement, or something else?
Jesus said something greater than Solomon is here. How does knowing Christ's wisdom and kingdom surpass even Solomon's glory change what you are seeking most eagerly in your own life right now?
Solomon's reign, however glorious, still ended after forty years. What legacy do you want to leave that will outlast your own lifetime?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote notes that the Septuagint and Syriac, matching 1 Kings 10:5, read and his burnt offerings that he presented, while the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads and his stairway by which he went up, a textual variant reflected in the translation choice.

Tarshish is generally understood as a distant western port, possibly in the western Mediterranean, and ships of Tarshish came to describe large, ocean going trading vessels generally, not necessarily ships bound specifically for that port.

The Chronicler cites three named prophetic sources, Nathan, Ahijah, and Iddo, for further records of Solomon's reign, none of which have survived as independent texts, distinct from the biblical books that bear similar prophetic names.
